title: How OLMo From The AI2 Redefines LLM Innovation
text:
The Allen Institute for AI created the Open Language Model, or OLMo, which is an open-source large language model with the aim of advancing the science of language models through open research. It marks a major milestone in the evolution of large language models.
Unlike current open large language models like Llama and Mistral, which might limit access to their training data, architectures, or evaluation methodologies, OLMo stands out by providing full access to its pre-training data, training code, model weights, and evaluation suite. This openness is aimed at empowering academics and researchers to collectively study and advance the field of language modeling.
OLMo represents a collaborative effort to advance the science of language models. The developers behind the LLM have a mission to empower academics and researchers by providing access to training code, models, and evaluation code necessary for open research.
OLMo's architecture is built on AI2’s Dolma dataset, which features a three trillion-token open corpus. It includes full model weights for four model variants at the 7B scale, each trained to at least 2T tokens. OLMo's innovative aspects include its training approaches, size, and the diversity of data it was trained on. Unique features that set it apart from predecessors are its open-source nature and the comprehensive release of training and evaluation tools.
OLMo's key differentiators include:
Full Pre-training Data and Code: OLMo is built on AI2's Dolma dataset, featuring a three trillion token open corpus that spans a diverse mix of web content, academic publications, code, books, and encyclopedic materials. This dataset is publicly available, allowing researchers to understand and leverage the exact data used for model training.
Comprehensive Framework Release: The framework includes not just the model weights but also the training code, inference code, training metrics, and logs for four model variants at the 7B scale. It even provides over 500 checkpoints per model for in-depth evaluation, all under the Apache 2.0 License.
Evaluation and Benchmarking Tools: AI2 has released Paloma, a benchmark for evaluating language models across various domains. This enables standardized performance comparisons and deeper insights into model capabilities and limitations.
In contrast to its contemporaries like Llama and Mistral, which have made significant contributions to the AI landscape through their respective advances and specializations, OLMo's commitment to openness and transparency sets a new precedent. It promotes a collective and transparent approach to understand, improve, and ethically advance the capabilities of language models.
The development of OLMo by the AI2 is a collaborative effort involving partnerships with several organizations and institutions. AI2 has teamed up with AMD and CSC, utilizing the GPU portion of the all-AMD processor-powered LUMI pre-exascale supercomputer. This collaboration extends to the hardware and computing resources necessary for the development of OLMo.
AI2 has partnered with organizations such as Surge AI and MosaicML for data and training code. These partnerships are crucial for providing the diverse datasets and sophisticated training methodologies that underpin OLMo's capabilities. The collaboration with the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Washington and Databricks Inc. has also been pivotal in realizing the OLMo project.
It is important to note that the current architecture of OLMo is not the same as the models that power chatbots or AI assistants, which use instruction-based models. However, that’s on the roadmap. According to AI2, there will be multiple enhancements made to the model in the future. In the coming months, there are plans to iterate on OLMo by introducing different model sizes, modalities, datasets, and capabilities into the OLMo family. This iterative process is aimed at continuously improving the model's performance and utility for the research community.
OLMo's open and transparent approach, along with its advanced capabilities and commitment to continuous improvement, make it a major milestone in the evolution of LLMs.

title: The Bermuda Triangle Of Generative AI: Cost, Latency, And Relevance
text:
Building enterprise solutions with Generative AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4, Claude 2, and others, is akin to navigating the Bermuda Triangle, marked by three critical constraints: cost, latency, and relevance. Crossing any one of
the three can sink a project, wasting time and money.
Everyone is excited about the technology’s potential, but there are significant challenges yet to be overcome before it transforms businesses. There are strategies, however, that innovative companies are using to successfully deploy LLMs at scale - but they involve trade-offs among the three sides of the triangle. Lowering cost usually decreases relevance. increasing relevance usually increases cost and latency. Lowering latency is usually more costly Finding the right mix is an optimization problem.
First, there’s the cost of developing, training, and maintaining a foundation model. Few companies can afford building their own model from scratch and so they typically rely on models accessed through APIs, either closed source (e.g., OpenAI’s GPT-4, Google’s Gemini Pro, Anthropic’s Claude2) or open source (e.g., Meta’s Llama2).
Closed source models are typically the most effective and easiest to use, but accessing them comes with potentially significant costs, especially for the most performant ones. Each token generated by LLMs incurs a cost, and given LLMs’ tendency for verbose output, a significant portion of that money is wasted on redundant or irrelevant computation. Open-source models are typically less costly to use but require more engineering capabilities to deploy and maintain. The use of smaller models (e.g., GPT3.5 instead of GPT4) can also be a way to decrease usage costs but can negatively impact relevance.
The second dimension is latency. Because LLM providers themselves have limited compute, they restrict the number of tokens that can be processed per minute – so called rate limits. That means real-time processing is nearly impossible for large-scale applications that require processing millions of tokens per minute. Latency levels above a few seconds can significantly hinder the adoption of any AI-based application. There are ways to improve latency – such as leveraging private clouds to avoid “sharing” LLMs with other companies, but which increases cost; or using smaller models, which as described can negatively impact relevance.
The last, and most critical dimension is of course relevance. The ability of Generative AI systems to generate accurate, contextually appropriate, and useful output is essential for user adoption, and therefore business impact. Despite their impressive capabilities, LLMs often produce outputs that require significant post-processing to meet specific criteria. This dimension is also the hardest to measure, as it is often based on qualitative assessments.
Relevance can be improved by injecting more information into a model. This can be done through prompt engineering (giving the model the right context and instructions), Retrieval-Augmented Generation techniques (allowing models to access external information in a trusted knowledge library) or fine-tuning (training the large language model with additional datasets). Each of these methods has its pros and cons, but they all come at the expense of latency. Some, like fine-tuning, can be particularly costly, and can lock enterprises into a particular model – if they switch to another model, all the fine-tuning work is lost.
So how do companies navigate this Bermuda Triangle of Generative AI, balancing the computational power of the models with the speed, precision and applicability of their outputs?
Techniques like parallelizing requests across multiple older models, chunking up data, model distillation, and using less resource-intensive models can help. For example, instead of calling a single model during inference, companies may consider calling multiple models simultaneously, routing subtasks to less expensive models and saving the most expensive models for the most difficult or critical tasks. AI agents can also access other systems or tools through API's because some subtasks can be handled by simpler tools or techniques.
One solution BCG designed for a global consumer-facing company building a virtual assistant used such a hyper-parallelized architecture to optimize latency and cost efficiency. The architecture allows the system to make multiple LLM calls in parallel, reducing the response time to just seconds per answer.
User input is first classified to determine whether the LLM should provide an automatic answer or if it should use a category-specific business logic. Depending on the classification, the system retrieves relevant data from proprietary knowledge bases, such as product databases, customer care logs, conversational data from past interactions, and external services accessed through APIs, with different LLMs pulling specific data simultaneously to minimize latency. An LLM then uses the data to construct a response. To optimize cost, the company leverages a model-agnostic architecture, and switches between models depending on the task to be performed, using the cheapest model that performs the task at hand accurately.
Chunking is the process of breaking down extensive text data into smaller, manageable segments for efficient processing, ensuring semantic relevance and minimizing noise. Distillation is the process of training smaller models using larger LLMs, creating accessible, specialized models that require less training data while maintaining performance.
And remember, foundation models are not the Swiss Army knives of AI. Use cases that do not directly contribute to enhancing customer service, creating new revenue streams, or addressing specific business needs may not need generative AI at all.
By considering alternative strategies, enterprises can effectively harness the potential of generative AI. But no single solution exists - it requires optimizing architecture and workflows to balance cost and capability. Orchestrating LLMs, human oversight, and various AI tools into an efficient symphony is key. And the solutions remain iterative as technology shifts. The technology is changing fast, but confronting the tradeoffs is essential to avoid disappearing into the Bermuda Triangle of generative AI.

title: State AGs warn Biden AI order could centralize control over tech, be used for ‘political ends’
text:
FIRST ON FOX: A coalition of state attorneys general is warning that an executive order signed by President Biden last year on artificial intelligence could be used by the federal government to "centralize" government control over the emerging technology and that that control could be used for political purposes -- including censoring alleged "disinformation."
"The Executive Order seeks—without Congressional authorization—to centralize governmental control over an emerging technology being developed by the private sector. In doing so, the Executive Order opens the door to using the federal government’s control over AI for political ends, such as censoring responses in the name of combatting ‘disinformation,’" the coalition of 20 attorneys general, led by Utah AG Sean Reyes, said in a letter to Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo.
Biden signed the order in October, which established new standards for AI safety and included moves to protect privacy and protect workers and consumers. Specifically, it requires developers to share safety test results and other information with the government.
"In accordance with the Defense Production Act, the Order will require that companies developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests," the White House said at the time. "These measures will ensure AI systems are safe, secure, and trustworthy before companies make them public."
The White House also said the order is aimed at protecting Americans from AI-enabled fraud by establishing standards and best practices to differentiate between AI-generated and authentic content.
However, in a letter to the Commerce Dept. responding to a request for information from the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the AGs say the order created a "gatekeeping function" for the Commerce Department to supervise AI development and forces developers to submit to an "opaque and undemocratic process."
"We are further concerned that the Executive Order’s bureaucratic and nebulous supervisory process will discourage AI development, further entrench large tech incumbents, and do little to protect citizens," they say.
They also accuse the executive of creating a "governmental black box" by failing to disclose how the federal government will use the information provided.

"The reporting requirements appear to be merely a pretext for ensuring that the federal government can find out who is developing AI models, supervise that process, and exert pressure to bend those AI models to the administration’s liking," they say.
They also warn that the order will inject "partisan purposes" into decision-making, including by forcing designers to prove it can tackle "disinformation."
"NIST should not use its assignment under the Executive Order to push a partisan agenda of censorship," they say.
The attorneys general also say that the authority in the Defense Production Act contains no authority to regulate development, only to encourage the production of it, meaning the executive does not have the authority to regulate this technology.
The officials tell Raimondo that the issues relating to AI are "complex and important, but they must be addressed by our constitutional, democratic process, not by executive fiat." The Commerce Dept. did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

title: Council Post: Accelerating Business AI Capabilities: A Strategic Guide For The First Step
text:
Aslak is the CEO of Selfly Store, works with customers in 20+ countries generating more revenue with data and intelligent vending machines.
Legend has it that Walt Disney once found a cowboy strolling through Disneyland's Tomorrowland on his way to Frontierland, and he wasn't too pleased. Disney believed that such an incongruous sight could spoil the magical experience for guests. However, due to Disneyland's limited space, creating an underground tunnel system was impractical. Fast-forward to the planning of the new Walt Disney World in Florida, and engineers came up with a clever solution: the utilidors. These utility corridors were designed to keep behind-the-scenes park operations hidden from the view of visitors, ensuring a seamless and enchanting experience for everyone.
This ingenious approach behind their creation was not just about immediate needs but also about future-proofing the park. By establishing a flexible "platform," Disney ensured the ability to adapt to evolving requirements. Business leaders can apply a similar strategic approach when cultivating today's and tomorrow's AI capabilities. We can lay the groundwork for robust AI functionality by preparing our data collection processes, optimizing IT tools and more. Having a proactive stance to ensure your readiness to harness the advantages of AI can help both you and your business thrive in the evolving landscape of technological innovation.
In my own company, I have seen how the transformative potential of AI can be harnessed across various dimensions, from predicting consumer demand influenced by factors like weather conditions, holiday seasons and traffic patterns to identifying and promoting the most sought-after items. Moreover, AI can play a pivotal role in optimizing operational processes and mitigating human errors. Let's take a closer look at how business leaders can plan ahead to take full advantage of these benefits.
The Importance Of Proper Data Collection
To achieve the full potential of AI, your data collection should cover several angles and be in a format that makes it easy for your team to compare datasets to each other. At the same time, the data needs to be comprehensive enough for your company to get accurate interpretations with the help of AI.
For example, the foundation of Tesla's journey into autonomous driving lay in meticulous data collection. They constructed a platform where data could be collected in a format conducive to swift analysis and comparison. This gave them the ability to detect anomalies in the data to help identify potential issues or, in unfortunate cases, fatal accidents. Human intervention was used to scrutinize the data and video recordings to comprehend what transpired, updating the algorithms and teaching the computer vision to respond effectively in similar situations. In the same way, I recommend not only relying on diverse, constantly updated algorithms when collecting and analyzing data, but also maintaining a skilled human team to help ensure the AI achieves effective, human-centric results with that data.
Consider also Google, which collects vast amounts of data for AI analyses through various channels and services. User interactions with Google Search, YouTube, Gmail and other products generate valuable data points, including search queries, video views, email content and more. The company also utilizes tracking technologies, like cookies and pixels, to monitor user behavior across the web. By using a wide range of data collection sources, you can compile extensive datasets to fuel your AI algorithms, enabling the development of sophisticated models for a variety of tasks.
Where To Start
Embarking on an AI journey for your business should begin with a solid foundation in business understanding. This involves identifying the kind of information crucial for your company's decision-making, as well as recognizing where AI can unveil insights that may elude human analysis.
• Reputable Sources
One way to kick-start your data collection journey is to benchmark research studies within your industry. Identify relevant item-level reporting findings, and tailor your data collection accordingly. AI excels at recognizing patterns and detecting anomalies within extensive datasets, so by leveraging AI tools, you can efficiently sift through large amounts of data from these relevant studies, uncovering valuable insights that have the potential to significantly impact your business.
For example, my company did a study on some of our clients' intelligent vending machines that revealed that sales experienced a substantial monthly increase when both Pepsi and Coca-Cola were offered—an impactful revelation for the same location and nearly identical product assortment. This underscores the transformative power of AI-driven data analysis in uncovering trends that might otherwise go unnoticed.
• Data Understanding
When it comes to understanding data, precision is paramount. Move from top-level categories downward and build a pool of datasets to be analyzed. Consider the example of Pepsi sold in vending machines—in this case, you might go beyond the beverage category to include details like cola type, packaging and even refill data to enhance your AI's ability to extract valuable insights. The more granular the data, the more effectively AI can identify patterns and potentially forecast future trends to optimize revenue.
• Contextual Specificity
Part of the reason why self-driving cars can cover a wide range of potential issues is contextual specificity. For example, when teaching the AI to recognize animals obstructing the road, rather than simply searching for "animals," the focus shifts to training AI with a diverse dataset of animals—dogs, cats, moose, bears, birds, etc. This nuanced approach allows the AI to comprehend different scenarios, considering factors like movement patterns, speed and even the weight of various animals. Just as in autonomous driving, attention to detail can help empower your AI to make informed decisions swiftly.
Conclusion
In the midst of the AI revolution, where everyone seems to be embracing its potential, data collection and utilization can play a significant role in drawing meaningful conclusions. The power of AI lies in the quality and accuracy of the data it processes; incorrect or flawed data can lead to misguided conclusions. Therefore, before relying on AI-driven insights to shape your business decisions, it's paramount to establish a solid foundation in data accuracy.
Ensuring that the fundamentals are in place is essential for a successful AI integration. When the basics of data collection and usage align seamlessly, the advantages of AI can become truly transformative for a business. These are undeniably exciting times, and by embracing AI with a keen eye on data integrity, you can position your business to thrive in this dynamic era of innovation.

title: Firmen suchen händeringend „Chief AI Officer“ – wer den Job will, muss mehr können, als IT
text:
Die Rolle des „Chief AI Officer“ ist einer der angesagtesten KI-Jobs in der Unternehmenswelt.
Der Chief AI Officer überbrückt idealerweise die Lücke zwischen technischer KI-Expertise und Geschäftssinn.
Aber Führungskräfte sagen, dass es schwierig sein kann, den richtigen Kandidaten zu finden – und dass viele die Rolle nicht verstehen.
Dies ist eine maschinelle Übersetzung eines Artikels unserer US-Kollegen von Business Insider. Er wurde automatisiert übersetzt und von einem Redakteur überprüft.
Es gibt einen neuen Platz am C-Level-Tisch – und zwar für den Chief AI Officer.
Im Großen und Ganzen besteht dessen Aufgabe darin, die Kluft zwischen den entscheidenden Mikrodetails der Arbeit mit KI und der Makrostrategie des größeren Unternehmens zu überbrücken. Diese Aufgabe ist in der Unternehmenswelt in letzter Zeit sehr viel bekannter geworden. Denn Unternehmen suchen Rat, wie sie Künstliche Intelligenz – eine relativ neue Technologie – einsetzen können, um Zeit zu sparen und die Produktivität zu steigern.
Unternehmen aus allen Branchen – von der Personalabteilung bis zur Halbleiterindustrie – suchen aktiv nach KI-Beauftragten. Sie erwarten von ihnen, dass sie eine wichtige Rolle bei der Steuerung der Unternehmen in Richtung KI-Einführung spielen. Schließlich entwickelt sich die Landschaft weiterhin schnell. Das ist manchmal auch dringend nötig, denn viele CEOs scheinen nicht zu wissen, wie sie die Technologie einführen, in sie investieren oder sie effektiv nutzen sollen. Eine kürzlich von Accenture durchgeführte Umfrage unter 3400 Führungskräften ergab, dass nur 27 Prozent der Unternehmen bereit sind, generative KI zu nutzen.
Einige Unternehmen sind sich jedoch nicht sicher, was die Rolle beinhaltet und ob sie notwendig ist. Außerdem ist es schwierig, jemanden zu finden, der für diese Rolle geeignet ist, sagen Personalvermittler.
Technische Fähigkeiten reichen nicht aus, um ein Chief AI Officer zu werden
Unternehmen, die mehr in KI investieren wollen, fragen sich vielleicht: Müssen wir wirklich einen Chief AI Officer einstellen, wenn es bereits Datenwissenschaftler und Entwickler für maschinelles Lernen mit fundierten Kenntnissen gibt?
Die Antwort der meisten Experten lautet: Ja. Die Fähigkeiten, die mit der Datenanalyse und dem maschinellen Lernen verbunden sind, reichen nicht aus. Beim maschinellen Lernen handelt es sich um einen weiteren angesagten technischen Beruf. Es geht dabei darum, KI-Systeme zu entwerfen, zu entwickeln und zu trainieren, damit sie schließlich eigene Entscheidungen treffen können.
Greg Selker ist Geschäftsführer des Personalberatungsunternehmens Stanton Chase. Er ist der Meinung, dass der ideale KI-Beauftragte ein breites Spektrum an Aufgaben zu erfüllen hat. Dazu gehört das Verständnis für die Funktionsweise großer Sprachmodelle und deren Erstellung. Er muss aber auch wissen, wie diese KI-Modelle im gesamten Unternehmen angewendet werden können.
„Er kann kein Datenwissenschaftler sein, der seine Zeit mit dem Schreiben von Algorithmen verbringt“, so Selker gegenüber Business Insider. „Der Chief AI Officer wird eher an der Entwicklung der Anwendungen beteiligt sein, die das Large Language Model (LLM) nutzen werden.“
Chris Daigle ist CEO des KI-Beratungsdientes ChiefAIOfficer.com. Er sagte, dass die meisten seiner kleinen und mittleren Kunden keinen Entwickler für maschinelles Lernen oder Datenanalysten benötigen, um ihre eigenen LLMs zu erstellen. Sie brauchen lediglich eine Führungspersönlichkeit, die die derzeit verfügbaren KI-Tools versteht. Außerdem muss sie wissen, wie sie auf verschiedene Bereiche ihres Unternehmens angewendet werden können.
Ein Chief AI Officer muss das Unternehmen auf Makro- und Mikroebene verstehen
Die Stelle erfordert auch Fähigkeiten außerhalb der Informatik. Justin Kinsey ist Vorsitzender des Personalvermittlungsunternehmens SBT Industries. Er sagt, dass seine Kunden eine Führungskraft brauchen, die sich im ethischen Minenfeld des KI-Einsatzes zurechtfindet. Mit diesem Wissen könne man sicherstellen, dass Produktivitätssteigerungen auf sichere Weise erzielt werden. SBT Industries arbeitet derzeit mit zwei Halbleiterunternehmen zusammen, um KI-Verantwortliche einzustellen.
Strategisches Denken sei der Schlüssel zu dieser Rolle, sagten viele, ebenso wie Führungsqualitäten.
Ein Chat GPT-Kenner mit ein paar Automatisierungstricks im Ärmel weiß beispielsweise nicht unbedingt, wie man den KI-Chatbot zur Umgestaltung eines Unternehmens einsetzt, so Daigle. Stattdessen sollte der Chief AI Officer das Unternehmen auf Makro- und Mikroebene verstehen, bevor er generative KI darauf aufbaut.
Im Idealfall handelt es sich um eine „Mischung aus technischem Fachwissen, strategischer Vision und Führungsqualitäten“, so Kinsey gegenüber Business Insider.
Die Einstellung eines KI-Chefs ist ein schwieriges Unterfangen
Unternehmensleiter sagten gegenüber Business Insider, dass es schwierig sein kann, den perfekten Kandidaten zu finden, der alle Voraussetzungen für die Rolle des Chief AI Officer erfüllt.
„Die schiere Neuheit dieses Bereichs bedeutet, dass es eine Herausforderung ist, eine Führungspersönlichkeit zu finden, die bereits die Bandbreite an Fähigkeiten bewiesen hat, um in einer solchen Rolle erfolgreich zu sein“, sagte Kinsey.
Unternehmen müssen sich möglicherweise auch verpflichten, in diese Funktion zu investieren – was laut Selker von Stanton Chase teuer sein kann.
„Es bleibt abzuwarten, wie viele Unternehmen die Umsetzung der Strategien tatsächlich finanzieren werden – und auf welchem Niveau“, so der Personalberater über KI.
Unternehmen brauchen KI-Expertise, oder sie riskieren, zurückzubleiben
Nichtsdestotrotz sagen Personalberater, dass Unternehmen die Einstellung von KI-Führungskräften in Betracht ziehen sollten, wenn es ihnen ernst damit ist, ein KI-First-Unternehmen zu sein.
Zumindest sollten sie diese Rolle als eine Erweiterung des Chief Data Officer oder Chief Information Officer betrachten, so Selker. So wissen sie, wie KI auf einer systemischen Ebene eingesetzt werden kann.
Die Entwicklung einer KI-Strategie, die auf das gesamte Unternehmen angewandt werden kann, kann darüber entscheiden, ob ein Unternehmen den Anschluss verliert, sagte er.
„Wenn man sich darüber noch keine Gedanken gemacht hat, ist man aufgeschmissen“, so Selker.

title: Council Post: Beyond Efficiency And Budgets: How Generative AI Is Transforming UX
text:
Lucas Persona is Chief Digital Officer at CI&T, a digital transformation partner for global brands.
Wherever you look today, the rapid advancement of generative AI is creating a state of flux for most industries and their related disciplines. While benefits like efficiency gains and cost reductions are crystal clear, uncertainty surrounds the future of human experts alongside an ever-evolving creative and productive force like AI.
Like most creative and knowledge-based professionals, user experience (UX) designers are pondering how their skills will stay relevant in an era where tools like Figma can generate entire designs from simple inputs.
Yet this concern is far more nuanced than “Will AI replace us?”
Instead, the question becomes, “What new user experiences does AI make possible? And what are the best practices for such unchartered waters?”
Addressing Persistent UX Challenges
Perfecting UX has long been a reductionist challenge, with designers iterating through countless possibilities until they track down the best solution for most users. Until now, this scenario has worked well on the business level since the alternative was a never-ending development scope that was too expensive to pursue.
There’s no question that cost considerations are vital, but they limit the scope of creative exploration and personalization in UX. Budget constraints force designers to approach their craft through a rigid, step-by-step process that emphasizes "how" to improve UX rather than "why" users have particular objectives or "what" the end goal should look like.
With generative AI, the UX world has the opportunity for a radical departure from these traditional constraints, enabling us to create thousands of variations of apps, web interfaces or digital experiences that constantly adapt and evolve to user preferences.
The key is to embrace a transformative shift in mindset that goes beyond efficiency gains and cost reductions.
Continuous Adaptation: Next-Gen UX Personalization
The first shift in mindset recognizes that generative AI empowers UX professionals to create dynamic, responsive systems that adapt to user behavior and preferences in real time.
Instead of aiming for a catch-all design, UX professionals can now design around nuanced user behaviors and intents, likes and dislikes, and granular interactions like clicks and swipes. AI shifts the focus from a singular user experience to a spectrum accommodating diverse preferences and needs.
Take e-commerce, for example. Traditionally, UX designers meticulously map out every screen flow and user action, from searching to filtering results, then adapt accordingly to suit the majority of users. Right now, a search for something like “coffee” comes with toggle filters like brand, size or rating. Yet a more specific text search like "8 ounces of ground Brazilian coffee" yields the same functionality—present a broad category, then allow users to narrow it down. AI-powered searches can adapt and respond more organically, guiding users to the right products much faster.
AI also opens up new possibilities for creating more intuitive and personalized experiences. For instance, an automotive brand’s website could highlight vehicle features based on individual user preferences—a family-focused buyer might see safety features, while a sports car enthusiast sees performance metrics.
Moreover, an apparel brand could use AI-generated images to demonstrate clothing or products on models that mirror the customer's appearance or preferred style. Companies could base this feature on an individual’s browsing history and past purchases to ensure relevant sizing and fit representation in the images.
These examples are a far cry from an all-encompassing AI chatbot, which can actually dilute the user interface experience; they require flexible AI models that can adapt to user inputs backed by structured human guidance. The result is an intuitive, personalized experience for everyone.
Human Guidance In AI-Powered UX Design
Traditionally, UX designers have concentrated on creating something tangible, like wireframes, while contemplating the underlying purpose of the design. However, with AI tools capable of rapidly producing initial drafts, designers now need to think more strategically upfront about their objectives and desired outcomes.
UX professionals will need to meticulously plan whatever they ask AI to create to align closely with their vision. As a result, their role becomes about setting clear intentions to generate the best possible results.
For instance, in product descriptions, the content must resonate with user interests. A UX designer would need to define this objective and parameters for the AI to align with that goal. Over time, the effectiveness of this approach can be measured through user engagement or conversion rates, offering chances to reiterate and providing tangible proof of success.
Aside from the creative aspect of setting intent and objectives, there's the technical side of producing material components, which generative AI tools will increasingly handle. Designers will need to guide these tools and decide which of the myriad AI-generated materials to use—a crucial process and skill set as AI drives the cost of production toward zero.
The interaction between UX and development teams will also transform. Developers often act as translators, converting detailed UX instructions into code. But as UX embraces a more generative approach, the need for such detailed instructions goes away.
These factors influence the second mindset shift: reduce focus on detailed, prescriptive execution processes to think more about the reasoning behind a design. This new-found freedom will allow UX teams to prove, without a doubt, that they achieved their objectives, generated value and met organizational goals.
Generative UX: The Next Evolution
With rapid advancements in generative AI, crafting a user experience tailored perfectly for each individual is becoming increasingly feasible. UX professionals will become the tutors of these experiences, setting the foundation for AI tools to evolve and grow within specific boundaries.
The objective becomes less about delivering a “final UX” and more about a “learning UX” that can adapt on the fly and works from a foundation of “why” (the user needs and expectations) and “what” (the end goal; the final result).
As we see it, this incoming wave of generative UX will add a layer of sophistication that expands the creative canvas and transcends the capabilities of traditional UX solutions.
And UX professionals are vital to bring about that change.

title: Will 2024 Be The Year That Generative AI Comes To Financial Services?
text:
Much has been written about the impact generative AI technology and services like ChatGPT will have on a broad range of industries, including financial services. But for all of the hype around generative AI, when will consumers have a ChatGPT-like service within their financial services website and mobile app?
Many of the largest financial services firms have announced that they are working on internal and/or client-facing generative AI initiatives. For example, JPMorgan Chase
As I’ve learned from working with clients in the financial services industry and talking to peers in the industry, 2024 is shaping up to be the year where generative AI in financial services goes from theory to reality. We will see powerful generative AI assistants starting to appear within consumers’ financial services websites and apps. This matters because the financial services sector currently offers only very basic chatbot assistants running on outdated technology. The transition to generative AI assistants will fundamentally change the way the average consumer manages their money and interacts with financial services firms.
This article will first provide a detailed explanation of why the transition to generative AI assistants will have such a significant impact on the financial services industry. We’ll then discuss the “when” question in more detail and a possible timeline for when different financial services industries will start offering client-facing generative AI assistants.
Why will the transition to generative AI assistants transform the financial services industry?
The financial services industry currently offers consumers basic chatbot assistants. The average financial service chatbot can only handle straightforward account servicing questions.
The average financial services chatbot struggles to explain financial concepts, cannot assist with financial planning and budgeting, and does not provide advice or help with investing. The industry’s chatbots are primarily designed to handle relatively straightforward customer support needs, and are not advanced enough to serve as a true assistant or advisor.
In contrast, generative AI assistants can provide reasonably accurate answers to a wide range of financial questions. Generative AI assistants can explain financial concepts/rules, help with budgeting and financial planning, and even provide high-level advice and recommendations when prompted in the right way. Generative AI assistants can also hold a conversation in a somewhat natural way and can refer back to previous comments and discussions. The stilted rules-based chatbots currently offered by the industry cannot hold a conversation or understand references to previous discussions.
One could argue that client-facing generative AI assistants will create the first real "robo" advisor, as this technology can actually act more like a true automated financial assistant. For example, Google’s Bard generative AI assistant can address relatively niche topics, like helping San Francisco residents with home shopping or providing cross-border tax advice. And generative AI technology will only continue to improve over time.
The transition to more powerful generative AI assistants will profoundly alter the financial services industry. Over time, consumers will likely interact with their generative AI financial assistant as the first “port of call” instead of navigating around the website or mobile app. Generative AI will be able to handle straightforward questions and will provide high-level guidance, leaving human experts to focus on more value-add activity.
So, with that background on how generative AI will change the industry, the question becomes “when.” When will financial services websites and mobile apps start offering generative AI assistants to clients?
When will generative AI come to your brokerage, card, and bank account?
Broadly speaking, the banking, credit card, and self-directed brokerage industries are more responsive to competitive pressure and new technology. These financial services verticals tend to react relatively quickly to disruption - such as the rise of zero commission trading or innovative credit card perks that capture market share.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, the two most prominent examples of live client-facing generative AI assistants in financial services come from these three financial services verticals. American neobroker Public.com (Alpha) and Dutch Neobank Bunq (Finn) have both launched generative AI assistants. Public’s Alpha assistant can notably generate impressive commentary on stocks and the market. Bunq’s Finn assistant can perform detailed analysis of the client’s account, including granularity to the level of how much money the client spent on pizza in the prior year.
Wells Fargo (Fargo) and American Fintech Dave (DaveGPT) have also announced that they have developed a virtual assistant using generative AI, although in my testing these two assistants are fairly basic and can primarily only handle simple customer service-related questions. Presumably, the functionality for both assistants will become more advanced over the course of 2024.
Expect more bank, brokerage and card firms to launch client-facing generative AI assistants in 2024. By the end of the year, these sectors will go from a handful of examples to more widespread adoption, creating strong competitive pressure for laggards to respond with their own generative AI assistant.
According to Jason Mikula, Publisher of Fintech Business Weekly, “the excitement about generative AI-powered tools is evident, both in the number of financial services firms discussing the capabilities in earnings calls and launching beta features, but also in bottoms-up adoption from end consumers. ChatGPT attracted over one million users in just five days after the public launch. For financial services companies, there are, as always, opportunities, risks, and barriers. In particular, firms must be careful about how their assistant will handle questions seeking advice and recommendations.”
When will generative AI come to insurance, financial advisors, and workplace retirement plans?
To broadly generalize, the insurance, workplace retirement plan, and traditional financial advisor industries do not respond to major technological shifts quickly. All three of these verticals typically involve strong personal relationships and/or very slow sales cycles, so there is less competitive pressure to respond to the latest technological innovation.
That said, each of these financial verticals would benefit greatly from generative AI assistants, as service and support is a significant cost for each of these products. A generative AI assistant that can hold a conversation with clients and can provide high-level guidance would reduce the routine servicing burden on insurance agents, financial advisors, and plan administrators.
Overall, expect these three financial services verticals to move slower. While there may be early adopter exceptions, it will likely be a few years before the average insurance and workplace retirement plan website and mobile app includes a powerful generative AI assistant.
Generative AI is poised to transform financial services in 2024, and financial services firms must start the process of building a generative AI assistants today
Generative AI assistants are coming to financial services. It is a matter of when, not “if,” and 2024 is shaping up to be the year generative AI arrives in financial services. For financial services firms that have not started the process of developing a client-facing generative AI assistant, you must start the process now.
It may take your firm many months to align all stakeholders on the design and approach before a single line of code can be written. Therefore, it is better to start this process now than in reaction to competitive pressure later in the year. In order to help firms on this journey, next week I will publish a follow-up article that outlines how financial services firms can build a generative AI assistant.

title: iOS 18—Stunning New Features Will Change The Game For All iPhone Users
text:
Apple’s iOS 18 update is launching in a few months’ time and if you believe the newest reports, it’s going to be the biggest iPhone upgrade yet. That’s because iOS 18 will be packed with artificial intelligence (AI)-based features and other major enhancements that will change your iPhone more than ever before, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.
Better still, the launch of iOS 18 isn’t far off. Apple’s latest and greatest new iPhone operating system will be officially announced at its Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC) in June.
“I’m told that the new operating system is seen within the company as one of the biggest iOS updates—if not the biggest—in the company’s history,” Gurman wrote in his Power On newsletter. “With that knowledge, Apple’s developers conference in June should be pretty exciting.”
It’s an exciting prospect, so based on current evidence, here’s what you can expect from iOS 18 when it launches.
iOS 18 Includes New AI enhanced Features
AI is everywhere at the moment—and the technology is developing rapidly. Apple’s foray into AI for its iOS operating system was first highlighted by Bloomberg last year, when it emerged that the iPhone maker wanted its next software upgrade to be “ambitious and compelling.”
At the time, it emerged that Apple was halting work on iOS 18 to debug the software and improve performance. This would have been music to the ears of many Apple fans, who complain of bugs in Apple’s popular software which can often put them off upgrading their iPhones.
And apparently, Apple head of software engineering Craig Federighi says iOS 18—which is codenamed Crystal—is definitely heading in the direction Apple had planned.
Among the new features coming in iOS 18 are AI-enhanced Siri, indicating Apple is following in the footsteps of both Microsoft and Google, which have their own AI-based chatbots.
In iOS 18, it’s possible AI will help with Apple Music playlists as well as troubleshooting any iPhone issues. Your iPhone could also be enhanced through auto-completion and auto-summarizing features in Apple apps, powered by the firm’s Ajax large language model.
Apple’s AI focus was also highlighted by CEO Tim Cook on a recent earnings call—the Apple chief said AI tools would arrive “this year,” according to The Verge. “I think there’s a huge opportunity for Apple with generative AI,” Cook added.
However, Apple’s AI features will not suddenly appear all at once. While iOS 18 is going to be a huge update, many of the new features are actually earmarked for 2025.
What To Know About AI Ahead of iOS 18
It’s certainly an exciting technology and new reports about iOS 18 increase the anticipation further. But it’s also important to consider the risk posed by AI technology as it increasingly enters people’s lives.
So before you use AI chatbots, make sure you're aware of the privacy risks. By default, they need to collect a lot of data, so you should be careful what you tell them and ensure you read the privacy policy.
It’s likely Apple will launch new privacy features in iOS 18 too, so look out for them and make sure you enable them, paying particular attention to anything enhanced by AI.

title: Touchdown Technology: The Rise Of AI In American Football
text:
In the adrenaline-fueled arena of professional football, the quest for excellence is relentless. Teams across the National Football League (NFL) have increasingly turning to a groundbreaking ally in their pursuit of victory: artificial intelligence (AI). This revolutionary technology is reshaping the game, offering insights and strategies that were once the stuff of dreams.
AI: The New MVP in Football
AI’s entry into football marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter in the game. By harnessing the power of machine learning and data analytics, NFL teams are elevating their game plans, enhancing player performance, and creating unforgettable fan experiences. To begin with, one of the most impactful uses of AI in football is in strategic game planning. Teams like the Philadelphia Eagles and the San Francisco 49ers leverage AI to analyze vast amounts of game data. This deep analysis helps in understanding opponents' strategies, identifying patterns, and predicting future plays. Coaches are empowered with insights that guide them in making strategic decisions, from play-calling to defensive alignments.
In addition, AI's role in improving player performance and health is groundbreaking. The NFL’s partnership with Amazon Web Services (AWS) created the “Next Gen Stats” platform to exemplify this. Using sensors in equipment and the stadium, AI algorithms analyze player movements, providing insights on performance metrics like speed, distance, and acceleration. Teams like the Dallas Cowboys and the New England Patriots use this data to tailor training programs and minimize injury risks.
Furthermore, akin to the rise of sabermetrics in baseball, AI has revolutionized football talent scouting and recruitment. Teams embrace advanced algorithms to scout and evaluate talent more effectively. The Cleveland Browns, for example, are known for their data-driven approach in scouting, harnessing AI to assess player skills, performance history, and even psychological attributes.
Beyond the Game: Improving the Off-Field Experience
Football teams employ AI beyond the on-field needs of the game. Recognizing the benefits to fans and operations, the NFL has jumped into the beyond the field needs. Today, AI already extends its impact to the fans, transforming their personal experience of the game. From AI-powered apps providing real-time statistics and predictive game analysis to chat bots enhancing customer service, the fan experience is more immersive and interactive than ever. The NFL’s use of AI in enhancing broadcasts with real-time graphics and analytics further enriches the viewer experience and enables the commentators to engage fans at a depth never thought possible.
Likewise, AI is instrumental in optimizing business operations. Teams like the Pittsburgh Steelers use AI for dynamic ticket pricing, adjusting prices based on demand, opponent strength, and other factors. AI-driven marketing strategies are also being employed, targeting fans with personalized promotions and offers. In addition, many NFL teams take advantage of AI for workforce development, particularly getting new employees ready for the stadium environment.
The Human-AI Partnership
The most exciting aspect of AI in football is the synergy it creates between technology and human expertise. Coaches, players, and staff are not being replaced but enhanced. AI provides valuable insights, but the critical decisions remain in the capable hands of the human experts. This synergy has once again proven the immense benefits of hybrid intelligence to any type of enterprise.
The Future of Football with AI
The future of AI in football is brimming with possibilities. From virtual reality experiences that allow fans to feel like they are part of the game to advanced player analytics that could redefine training and strategy, the potential is boundless. For young athletes, coaches, and sports enthusiasts, AI’s rise in football opens a universe of opportunities. It is an invitation to be part of a transformative journey, to learn and adapt, and to be at the forefront of this exciting technological frontier.
In the end, football’s embrace of AI is a call to adventure. Far beyond technological advancement, teams and leagues seeking opportunities with A is a major a paradigm shift. For them, it is about pushing the boundaries of what is possible, both on and off the field. It’s about the harmonious blend of human ambition and machine intelligence. As we stand on the cusp of this new era of football, the call to adventure is clear. Through the power of AI, football professionals will transform the game, to reach new heights of excellence and to inspire a new generation players and fans. The future of football is a thrilling journey, where the spirit of football meets the power of AI, creating a game that’s more dynamic, more exciting, and more inspiring than ever before. The game is evolving, and with AI, we are all part of this magnificent transformation.

title: SAP BrandVoice: How Generative AI For Business Is Creating A New Playbook For Value
text:
Every technology conversation today centers around the transformative potential of generative AI for the future. But the reality is, it’s already happening today. And while its capabilities are noteworthy, the real promise of generative AI for business isn’t what it can do so much as the value it can create.
In my role at SAP, I speak to business leaders all the time about the value that generative AI can add to their business in ways they might not even realize, and I hear countless stories about how it’s already starting to do that. One of my favorite examples is one that SAP announced last week in an arena that is near and dear to me – finding and developing the next generation of star athletes.
As someone who used to play and coach basketball in Australia, I’ve had a lifelong appreciation of coaching but also of scouting talent. Scouting is a discipline where art truly meets science, where experience and intuition are strengthened by the objective reality revealed by data.
While professional scouting has been around for a very long time, as more data on players becomes available, more teams are using it as a competitive advantage. But that’s not as easy as it sounds. While the sophistication of scouting reports is impressive, the process of creating and using them effectively has never been efficient.
When you consider how many potential young star athletes there are in the world, you can see how this would create an enormous amount of scouting reports to go through in a short period of time. The problem gets even more daunting when you consider that they are written in different languages and in different writing styles. In short, it’s exactly the kind of challenge that generative AI for business is built to solve.
For proof of that, just look at the German professional soccer clubs FC Bayern Munich and Hertha BSC. For a long time, both clubs have employed talent scouts who travel the world watching matches and collecting reams of data about players in the hope of finding the next great star before any of their competitors do.
But to show how this could be done better, SAP collaborated with FC Bayern Munich and Hertha BSC on a prototype. It uses generative AI to create automated summaries and recommendations of the reports created by their different scouts in different parts of the world and makes them available to club executives simply by asking for them in their natural language.
For example, imagine a German-speaking manager of the club being able ask for a key summary in 100 words or less of a scouting report on a young player who was scouted in Argentina and written in Spanish. That same manager can also ask it to compare two players based on their just their defensive skills or endurance.
While translation apps can translate an entire report from Spanish to German, it takes a large language model to create these summaries and competitive analyses on demand using natural language commands – essentially just the information that club executives really need to make informed decisions fast.
This is exactly what the prototype allowed these clubs to do. It took a time-consuming task and automated it in an intelligent way to make it useful. As a result, we will soon be rolling out this capability as part of our SAP Sports One sports management suite, which has already been helping athletes and teams get better results in their sport while also creating better experiences for their fans since 2015.
Why should business leaders care about better scouting reports? Two reasons. First, because they face many of the same challenges in their own business, needing to harness the power of their data quickly on demand for competitive advantage. And two, because generative AI isn’t just a specific solution for a specific problem.
Its true magic is that it’s also scalable across an entire enterprise to address other business needs from financing and supply chain management to procurement, travel, trainings, and more. For example, when generative AI is combined with SAP’s Business Technology Platform, businesses have the ability to write code, keeping their core clean and building generative AI extensions to further scale it’s impact.
There is simply no doubt that data is the playbook of champions in sports. But it is also creating a new playbook of value in business. And with the era of generative AI for business only just beginning, I cannot wait to see what other amazing innovations will move from imagination to reality – and all of the value that they will create.

Nvidia hits record high as Goldman Sachs boosts price target on AI prospects
Nvidia's shares scaled a new peak on Monday after Goldman Sachs raised its price target for the high-flying chipmaker's stock in anticipation of a major boost to its earnings from the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
Nvidia's shares scaled a new peak on Monday after Goldman Sachs raised its price target for the high-flying chipmaker's stock in anticipation of a major boost to its earnings from the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
The stock rose about 4% to $689.21 and looked set to add about $70 billion to the company's market capitalization. Nvidia was valued at $1.63 trillion as of Friday's close.
Nvidia has emerged as a poster child of the AI frenzy and saw a record monthly jump in its market value in January.
The searing growth in the stock price - already up about 39% so far this year - has made it more expensive to own relative to its peers. Nvidia's shares trade at 31.4 times the company's forward earnings estimate, compared with the industry average of 22.9.
Still, Goldman Sachs analyst Toshiya Hari sees more room for growth.
"We believe Nvidia will remain as the industry gold standard for the foreseeable future, given its robust hardware and software offerings and, importantly, the pace at which it continues to innovate," Hari said.
Goldman Sachs analysts raised their price target for Nvidia to $800, the third highest among U.S. analysts covering the stock and indicating a 21% upside from current levels, according to LSEG data. Its previous price target was $625.
The bank also lifted its full-year 2025-2026 earnings estimates for Nvidia by 22% on an average, citing signs of robust AI server demand and improving graphics processing unit (GPU) supply.
Hari pointed to signs of AI monetization from companies including Microsoft and Meta Platforms as well as positive earnings outlook from AI server maker Super Micro Computer.
While Nvidia has unlocked billions in revenue on the back of the AI frenzy, other chipmakers that are not so deeply involved in making chips for AI, such as Intel, have seen their shares lag.
Nvidia is set to report results on Feb. 21, with analysts expecting fourth-quarter earnings per share of $4.51 and revenue of $20.19 billion, according to LSEG data.
